content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has prioritized the definition and promotion of universal access to healthy and sustainable diets. This involves identifying key actions, developing guidelines, supporting implementation, and monitoring progress. These efforts aim to address issues such as undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight, obesity, and diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs), while also preserving biodiversity and planetary health. WHO and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) have established guiding principles for sustainable healthy diets, emphasizing the central role of biodiversity. Biodiversity is directly or indirectly linked to all 16 principles identified for sustainable diets. These principles align with broader goals of mainstreaming sustainability into food systems. Scientific and policy communities have increasingly recognized sustainable diets and food systems as critical pathways to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Evidence suggests that reducing per capita consumption of ruminant meat and shifting toward plant-based diets rich in fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, and legumes can improve nutrition, reduce biodiversity pressures, and mitigate climate change. However, dietary recommendations must be tailored to local contexts, as some populations may require increased meat consumption to meet nutritional needs. Plant-based diets have demonstrated benefits for weight management, energy metabolism, and reducing systemic inflammation in healthy individuals, as well as in those with obesity or type 2 diabetes. Emerging research highlights the potential of plant-based diets to positively influence gut microbiome diversity, opening avenues for innovative preventive and therapeutic strategies against obesity and related comorbidities. Food processing can enhance diet quality by improving food availability and safety. However, certain processing methods result in high levels of salt, added sugars, and saturated fats, which, when consumed excessively, undermine dietary quality. Efforts to minimize the use of plastics in food packaging and promote clean drinking water as the preferred fluid are also essential components of sustainable diets. The global food system is a major determinant of health and sustainable development. Comprehensive scientific reports underscore the urgent need for its transformation to achieve sustainability goals. This requires coordinated policies and strategies that address the interconnectedness of biodiversity, agriculture, water, diets, and greenhouse gas emissions. Cross-sectoral collaboration, knowledge exchange, and alignment of global goals with local implementation are critical to this transformation. Indicators for biodiversity, nutrition, and health integration are being developed to assess the resilience of food production landscapes and seascapes. These indicators aim to provide technical support and evidence for addressing biodiversity loss in food systems, assessing the sustainability of health services, and identifying entry points for policies that promote healthy diets and reduce diet-related illnesses. Field testing of these indicators is prioritized in communities heavily reliant on biodiversity and ecosystem services, with high burdens of malnutrition or diet-related NCDs. The ultimate goal is to mainstream biodiversity into nutrition and health strategies, ensuring coherence across sectors and alignment with international commitments such as the SDGs and the Paris Climate Agreement. This requires robust public policies, political will, private sector partnerships, and investments in sustainable diets, supported by disaggregated data and technological innovation.
